title: Collapse after a wasp sting — recognise danger, assess and act safely

blocks.text: Collapse after a wasp sting — recognise danger, assess and act safely

AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · R5-212 · Station 2 acute consultation · 20 minutes · Assessed skills: A clinical assessment, B physical signs where appropriate, C communication, D differential diagnosis, E clinical judgement, F patient concerns, G welfare · Not an official PACES mark scheme.

A patient has recovered after emergency treatment for collapse, wheeze and widespread urticaria following a wasp sting. Conduct the follow-up consultation before discharge. You are the medical registrar in the acute assessment unit (or appropriately designated acute clinician). Explore concerns, assess risk and explain the immediate plan.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected venom-triggered anaphylaxis after emergency stabilisation. Examiner trap: Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline.

rows: “First I need to check you are safe.”
“I will ask a few focused questions.”

Confirm timing of sting and airway, breathing and circulatory compromise, adrenaline response and previous sting reactions. Check whether symptoms have completely resolved and the observation plan is appropriate.
“I will explain the likely problem and alternatives.”
Suspected venom-triggered anaphylaxis after emergency stabilisation.

Apply NICE NG258 risk-based observation and discharge criteria. Supply two adrenaline auto-injectors, demonstrate brand-specific use, explain positioning and emergency-service contact, and refer to specialist allergy for venom assessment and possible immunotherapy.
Ignores renewed wheeze, collapse or hypotension
Checks present breathing/circulation and evidence of ongoing or recurrent anaphylaxis
Interrupts consultation to trigger emergency ABCDE and adrenaline if new ABC compromise
Labels a simple local sting reaction as anaphylaxis without checking symptoms
Establishes timing of sting, airway, breathing, circulation, rash, treatment received and response
Checks previous reactions, asthma, co-factors, and exposure risk for allergy referral
Explains likely systemic venom-triggered anaphylaxis based on prior collapse and wheeze
Differentiates vasovagal syncope and isolated urticaria while emphasising emergency features
Offers antihistamine first for airway compromise
In recurrent adult anaphylaxis gives 500 micrograms IM adrenaline into lateral thigh promptly, calls for help and repeats after 5 minutes if symptoms persist
Positions safely, gives oxygen and monitored crystalloid resuscitation where needed; avoids IV adrenaline outside expert setting
Delays adrenaline for tryptase or discharges despite symptoms
Considers timed tryptase where still applicable; uses individualised risk-based observation, documented safety assessment
Explains no single test confirms anaphylaxis and specialist interpretation and follow-up are needed
Discharges without adrenaline autoinjectors or instruction
Provides two adrenaline autoinjectors, demonstration, written emergency plan and safety-netting
Arranges allergy specialist referral for venom testing and consideration of venom immunotherapy
Promises all sting reactions warrant desensitisation
Addresses fear, teaches device use, when to call emergency services and when recurrence merits urgent action
Uses teach-back and clarifies that specialist testing determines immunotherapy eligibility

blocks.text: Patient is anxious but cooperative. Open with: “I am worried something serious is happening.” Answer history questions using these facts only: Confirm timing of sting and airway, breathing and circulatory compromise, adrenaline response and previous sting reactions. Check whether symptoms have completely resolved and the observation plan is appropriate. Ask “Will I need to stay in hospital?” and accept calm, specific explanations. No unscripted extra examination findings.
Q5. Does every sting require venom immunotherapy? MODEL: No. Specialist evaluation determines whether venom testing and immunotherapy are indicated.
Q4. What must discharge cover? MODEL: Risk-based observation, two autoinjectors with teaching, written emergency plan and specialist allergy referral.
Q3. Are antihistamines a substitute for adrenaline? MODEL: No. They do not treat life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problems.

Q2. What if wheeze/hypotension returns? MODEL: Stop consultation, urgent ABCDE, IM adrenaline 500 micrograms adult dose into lateral thigh, repeat after 5 minutes if needed, summon resuscitation help.
Q1. What was the likely diagnosis? MODEL: Systemic venom-triggered anaphylaxis given the history of sting followed by wheeze and cardiovascular collapse.

FAIL — CANDIDATE: “It is probably fine; I will ask my routine questions first.” [R1/R3 Fail] PATIENT: “I feel worse.” CANDIDATE: “We can reassess tomorrow.” [R6/R7 Fail] EXAMINER: “Your diagnosis and differential?” CANDIDATE: “I am not sure; perhaps anxiety.” [R2/R4 Fail] EXAMINER: “Investigations?” CANDIDATE: “Everything routinely.” [R5 Fail] Examiner note: missed the immediate safety decision.

PASS — CANDIDATE: “I’m the doctor looking after you. I’ll assess your immediate safety, then explain what we need to do.” [R1/R3 Pass] CANDIDATE: “Confirm timing of sting and airway, breathing and circulatory compromise, adrenaline response and previous sting reactions. Check whether symptoms have completely resolved and the observation plan is appropriate.” [R2 Pass] EXAMINER: “Your impression?” CANDIDATE: “Suspected venom-triggered anaphylaxis after emergency stabilisation.” [R4 Pass] EXAMINER: “Tests?” CANDIDATE: “Document onset and treatment. Arrange appropriately timed mast-cell tryptase if still in the sampling window, with possible baseline test at allergy follow-up; testing does not delay treatment.” [R5 Pass] EXAMINER: “Treatment?” CANDIDATE: “Apply NICE NG258 risk-based observation and discharge criteria. Supply two adrenaline auto-injectors, demonstrate brand-specific use, explain positioning and emergency-service contact, and refer to specialist allergy for venom assessment and possible immunotherapy.” [R6 Pass] PATIENT: “Am I in danger?” CANDIDATE: “Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline. I will explain each step and check your questions.” [R7 Pass] Examiner note: safe priorities and clear explanation.

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “I can see you are uncomfortable. Before anything else I will check breathing, circulation, pain and your priorities.” [R1/R3 High-performance] CANDIDATE: “I want to identify what changed and which associated findings increase risk: Confirm timing of sting and airway, breathing and circulatory compromise, adrenaline response and previous sting reactions. Check whether symptoms have completely resolved and the observation plan is appropriate.” [R2 High-performance] EXAMINER: “What else could this be?” CANDIDATE: “Suspected venom-triggered anaphylaxis after emergency stabilisation. I will not anchor on this label if the examination suggests a competing emergency.” [R4 High-performance] EXAMINER: “Prioritise.” CANDIDATE: “Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline. This means I will act without waiting for delayed confirmatory results. Document onset and treatment. Arrange appropriately timed mast-cell tryptase if still in the sampling window, with possible baseline test at allergy follow-up; testing does not delay treatment.” [R5 High-performance] CANDIDATE: “Apply NICE NG258 risk-based observation and discharge criteria. Supply two adrenaline auto-injectors, demonstrate brand-specific use, explain positioning and emergency-service contact, and refer to specialist allergy for venom assessment and possible immunotherapy. I will document response and involve the appropriate specialists.” [R6 High-performance] PATIENT: “I am frightened.” CANDIDATE: “I will explain why we recommend these steps, hear your preferences, and tell you exactly what would make us change the plan.” [R7 High-performance] Examiner note: prioritised reasoning with responsive communication.

R2/R4: Inadequate discriminatory history: Confirm timing of sting and airway, breathing and circulatory compromise, adrenaline response and previous sting reactions. Check whether symptoms have completely resolved and the observation plan is appropriate.

R5/R6: Orders investigation without initiating the urgent action: Apply NICE NG258 risk-based observation and discharge criteria. Supply two adrenaline auto-injectors, demonstrate brand-specific use, explain positioning and emergency-service contact, and refer to specialist allergy for venom assessment and possible immunotherapy.

R7: Omits the specific hazard: Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline.
“I should first check whether the patient is physiologically stable.”
“A key competing possibility must be considered before attributing all symptoms to one diagnosis.”

“The immediately preventable harm here is: Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline.”

Suspected venom-triggered anaphylaxis after emergency stabilisation. Document onset and treatment. Arrange appropriately timed mast-cell tryptase if still in the sampling window, with possible baseline test at allergy follow-up; testing does not delay treatment. Apply NICE NG258 risk-based observation and discharge criteria. Supply two adrenaline auto-injectors, demonstrate brand-specific use, explain positioning and emergency-service contact, and refer to specialist allergy for venom assessment and possible immunotherapy. Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline.

THINK: Suspected venom-triggered anaphylaxis after emergency stabilisation. SAY: name and explain urgency. DO: Apply NICE NG258 risk-based observation and discharge criteria. Supply two adrenaline auto-injectors, demonstrate brand-specific use, explain positioning and emergency-service contact, and refer to specialist allergy for venom assessment and possible immunotherapy. NUMBERS: 20-minute PACES consultation. TRAP: Warn about recurrent/biphasic symptoms: use auto-injector immediately for airway, breathing or circulation symptoms and call emergency services; do not stand suddenly after adrenaline. FINISH: reassess and safety-net.
